{\LARGE\bfseries\sffamily\color{AtlasNavy} Lipschitz convex optimization with exact values\par}\vspace{5pt}
\textbf{Setting ID.} \texttt{SO\_\allowbreak{}\allowbreak{}ZO\_\allowbreak{}\allowbreak{}E01}

Single-objective optimization

Minimize \AtlasInlineMath{f} globally over \AtlasInlineMath{B_2(0,R)} and return a point with small objective gap.

\textbf{Status.} Logarithmic gap present

\textbf{TASK tags.} formulation: Global minimization; solution concept: Global minimization; task family: Single objective

\textbf{MODEL tags.} convexity: Convex; smoothness: Lipschitz function; structure: No additional structure

\textbf{ORACLE tags.} access order: Zeroth-order interface; interface family: Exact value; public information: Public inputs explicitly declared; operation: Function value; feedback quality: Exact

\textbf{ALGORITHMS tags.} adaptivity: Adaptive; randomization: Deterministic algorithms; randomization: Private randomness allowed; restriction: No additional span restriction explicitly imposed

\textbf{OUTPUT tags.} certificate: No additional output certificate required

\textbf{METRIC tags.} criterion: Objective gap

\textbf{GUARANTEE tags.} aggregation: Per instance; mode: Deterministic; mode: Probability

\textbf{RESOURCE tags.} budget: Fixed worst-case budget

\needspace{7\baselineskip}\section{1. Setting specification}
\needspace{4\baselineskip}\subsection{Task}
Minimize \AtlasInlineMath{f} globally over \AtlasInlineMath{B_2(0,R)} and return a point with small objective gap.

\needspace{4\baselineskip}\subsection{Admissible model}
\AtlasInlineMath{f:B_2(0,R)\to\mathbb{R}} is convex and satisfies \AtlasInlineMath{|f(x)-f(y)|\le L\|x-y\|_2} for every \AtlasInlineMath{x,y} in the ball. Neither a definition nor regularity outside the ball is assumed. Continuity on the ball guarantees attainment of the constrained minimum.

\needspace{4\baselineskip}\subsection{Oracle interface}
At any finite query point \AtlasInlineMath{x} in \AtlasInlineMath{B_2(0,R)}, the oracle returns the single exact scalar \AtlasInlineMath{f(x)}. The reply is uniquely determined and contains no gradient, subgradient or derivative-vector product.

Projection and the stated proximal operations over known geometry are free.

The public inputs are \AtlasInlineMath{d}, \AtlasInlineMath{L}, \AtlasInlineMath{R}, \AtlasInlineMath{\varepsilon}, together with the sets, kernels and auxiliary operations explicitly declared above. Information about the unknown objective and any undisclosed sample distribution is obtained only through the stated interface.

\needspace{4\baselineskip}\subsection{Output}
Return \AtlasInlineMath{\widehat{x}\in B_2(0,R)}. The output may be an unqueried point, an average or convex combination that remains in the stated space. No function value, gradient, inner solution, or accuracy certificate must accompany the output.

\needspace{4\baselineskip}\subsection{Loss or accuracy criterion}
The base loss is \AtlasInlineMath{\ell(I,x)=f(x)-f_*}, where \AtlasInlineMath{f_*=\inf_{u\in B_2(0,R)}f(u)}. This nonnegative loss is evaluated at the output, with tolerance \AtlasInlineMath{\varepsilon}.

\needspace{4\baselineskip}\subsection{Resource accounting}
Each scalar function value or noisy observation costs \AtlasInlineMath{1} call. Every location in a multipoint finite difference, every initialization query, and every reference observation is charged.

Only the declared oracle resource is charged. Computation and storage using existing information, together with explicitly known geometric and proximal operations, are free.

\needspace{4\baselineskip}\subsection{Algorithm views and success guarantees}
\needspace{4\baselineskip}\subsubsection{Deterministic}
Only deterministic strategies are allowed. Queries, stopping and postprocessing may be arbitrary measurable adaptive functions of the history. No linear-span or zero-respecting restriction is imposed.

Interactions are sequential, and every actual response in a batch is charged separately. Except for explicitly listed auxiliary interfaces, arithmetic, linear algebra, storage, and internal computation on available information are free, with no additional communication or memory restriction. Finite-difference steps must be finite and positive; real-number precision is not charged separately.

After fixing the public inputs, choose one algorithm that works for every admissible instance and reply law. The requirement \AtlasInlineMath{\ell(I,\widehat{x})\le \varepsilon} holds deterministically for each instance.

Oracle cost uses a deterministic worst-case budget: \AtlasInlineMath{N\le T} on every possible execution path. For multiple resources, coordinatewise caps apply jointly along the same path.

\needspace{4\baselineskip}\subsubsection{Randomized}
Private randomization is allowed, with the seed independent of the instance and external randomness. Queries, stopping and postprocessing may be arbitrary measurable adaptive functions of the history. No linear-span or zero-respecting restriction is imposed.

Interactions are sequential, and every actual response in a batch is charged separately. Except for explicitly listed auxiliary interfaces, arithmetic, linear algebra, storage, and internal computation on available information are free, with no additional communication or memory restriction. Finite-difference steps must be finite and positive; real-number precision is not charged separately.

After fixing the public inputs, choose one algorithm that works for every admissible instance and reply law. The error requirement is \AtlasInlineMath{\Pr(\ell(I,\widehat{x})\le \varepsilon)\ge2/3}.

Probability is over the algorithm's random seed only.

Oracle cost uses a deterministic worst-case budget: \AtlasInlineMath{N\le T} on every possible execution path. For multiple resources, coordinatewise caps apply jointly along the same path.

\textbf{Output qualification.} Random selection among previously queried points is permitted, subject to the declared success guarantee.

Includes the unknown objective and its admissible feedback distribution or environment law. Public parameters are fixed before the quantifiers.

\AtlasInlineMath{\mathcal{I}}: Admissible instance class determined by the eight specification fields in this profile \textbf{Domain:} Instances satisfying the public parameter bounds.

\AtlasInlineMath{\mathcal{A}}: Algorithm or strategy \textbf{Domain:} Measurable adaptive strategies allowed in this profile.

The algorithm is selected before the hidden instance.

\AtlasInlineMath{\ell}: Base loss or residual \textbf{Domain:} \AtlasInlineMath{\ell:\mathcal{I}\times\mathcal{X}_{\mathrm{out}}\to[0,+\infty]}.

The exact formula appears in this profile's performance-criterion section.

\AtlasInlineMath{\mathbb{E},\Pr}: Expectation and probability \textbf{Domain:} Evaluated over the algorithmic and feedback randomness specified by this profile's guarantee.

Fix the instance first; aggregate cost and error separately.

\AtlasInlineMath{\inf,\sup}: Infimum and supremum \textbf{Domain:} Evaluated only over the variable sets explicitly specified in the formula.

In the risk definition, the infimum over algorithms precedes the supremum over instances or centers.

\AtlasInlineMath{\|\cdot\|_2,\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle}: Euclidean norm and inner product \textbf{Domain:} \AtlasInlineMath{\|x\|_2=\sqrt{\langle x,x\rangle}}.

\AtlasInlineMath{\langle x,y\rangle=x^\top y}

\AtlasInlineMath{B_p(c,R)}: Closed norm ball \textbf{Domain:} \AtlasInlineMath{p\in[1,\infty],\ R\ge0}.

\AtlasInlineMath{B_p(c,R)=\{x:\|x-c\|_p\le R\}}; \AtlasInlineMath{B_2} denotes the Euclidean ball.

\AtlasInlineMath{N,T}: Actual call count and declared budget \textbf{Domain:} \AtlasInlineMath{N,T\in\mathbb{N}_0}.

A fixed budget bounds every execution path; the Markov specification uses an expected budget.

\AtlasInlineMath{O,\Omega,\Theta,\widetilde{O}}: Asymptotic upper bounds, lower bounds, matching orders, and upper bounds with hidden logarithms \textbf{Domain:} Within the joint parameter window specified for each complexity regime.

Dependence of hidden constants on fixed parameters is stated separately for each bound. Tilde notation may hide logarithmic factors only in the declared variables.

\AtlasInlineMath{c,C,c_\alpha,C_\alpha}: Positive constant in a proof or asymptotic bound \textbf{Domain:} \AtlasInlineMath{0<c,C,c_\alpha,C_\alpha<\infty}.

Unsubscripted constants have the dependencies stated in the bound; constants subscripted by \AtlasInlineMath{\alpha} may depend only on the fixed smoothness order.

\AtlasInlineMath{\log,\log_+,e}: Natural logarithm, truncated logarithm, and Euler's number \textbf{Domain:} \AtlasInlineMath{z>0}.

\AtlasInlineMath{\log_+(z)=\max\{0,\log z\}}; \AtlasInlineMath{e=\exp(1)}, and \AtlasInlineMath{\log_2} denotes the base-two logarithm.

\AtlasInlineMath{f,f_*}: Population objective and its optimal value \textbf{Domain:} \AtlasInlineMath{f:\mathcal{X}_{\mathrm{fun}}\to\mathbb{R}}.

\AtlasInlineMath{f_*=\inf_{x\in B_2(0,R)}f(x)}.

\AtlasInlineMath{\mathcal{X}_{\mathrm{fun}},\mathcal{X}_{\mathrm{out}},\mathcal{X}}: Function domain, admissible output domain and optimization domain \textbf{Domain:} Each is the Euclidean space or subset explicitly specified in this profile.

\AtlasInlineMath{\mathcal{X}_{\mathrm{out}}=B_2(0,R)} and \AtlasInlineMath{\mathcal{X}=B_2(0,R)}; the function domain is the region on which the model imposes regularity.

\AtlasInlineMath{N^*}: Optimal worst-case oracle complexity satisfying the complete guarantee \textbf{Domain:} \AtlasInlineMath{N^*\in[0,+\infty]}.

Take the infimum over admissible algorithms, followed by the worst case over the instances of this profile. With multiple resources, use this scalar only for an explicitly specified resource projection.

\begingroup\raggedright\sloppy A deterministic procedure obtains an \$\textbackslash{}eta\$-accurate subgradient at a point within distance \$\textbackslash{}zeta\$ of the requested point using at most \$7d\textbackslash{}lceil\textbackslash{}log\_\allowbreak{}2(2L\textbackslash{}sqrt d/\allowbreak{}\textbackslash{}eta)\textbackslash{}rceil\$ values. It yields the convex upper \$O(dA\textasciicircum{}2\textbackslash{}log(edA))\$ and the strongly convex upper \$O(dL\textasciicircum{}2\textbackslash{}log(edA)/\allowbreak{}(\textbackslash{}mu\textbackslash{}varepsilon))\$,\allowbreak{} with \$A=\allowbreak{}LR/\allowbreak{}\textbackslash{}varepsilon\$.\newline{}\newline{}For a convex one-dimensional restriction,\allowbreak{} maintain an active interval whose every subderivative lies in \$[\textbackslash{}ell,\allowbreak{}u]\$. Divide it into six equal pieces and query its seven grid points. Their secant slopes satisfy \$s\_\allowbreak{}0\textbackslash{}le\textbackslash{}cdots\textbackslash{}le s\_\allowbreak{}5\$. The intervals \$[q\_\allowbreak{}1,\allowbreak{}q\_\allowbreak{}2]\$ and \$[q\_\allowbreak{}4,\allowbreak{}q\_\allowbreak{}5]\$ have protected subgradient envelopes \$[s\_\allowbreak{}0,\allowbreak{}s\_\allowbreak{}2]\$ and \$[s\_\allowbreak{}3,\allowbreak{}s\_\allowbreak{}5]\$. Since \$(s\_\allowbreak{}2-s\_\allowbreak{}0)+(s\_\allowbreak{}5-s\_\allowbreak{}3)\textbackslash{}le u-\textbackslash{}ell\$,\allowbreak{} selecting the narrower one halves the envelope width and divides the interval length by six.\newline{}\newline{}Set \$\textbackslash{}tau=\allowbreak{}\textbackslash{}eta/\allowbreak{}\textbackslash{}sqrt d\$,\allowbreak{} \$k=\allowbreak{}\textbackslash{}lceil\textbackslash{}log\_\allowbreak{}2(2L/\allowbreak{}\textbackslash{}tau)\textbackslash{}rceil\$,\allowbreak{} and \$r\_\allowbreak{}1=\allowbreak{}\textbackslash{}zeta/\allowbreak{}2\$. At coordinate \$j\$,\allowbreak{} run \$k\$ subdivisions from half-width \$r\_\allowbreak{}j\$,\allowbreak{} move to the final midpoint,\allowbreak{} and retain the two protected secants of denominator \$h\_\allowbreak{}j=\allowbreak{}2r\_\allowbreak{}j6\textasciicircum{}\{-k\}\$. Set \$r\_\allowbreak{}\{j+1\}=\allowbreak{}\textbackslash{}tau h\_\allowbreak{}j/\allowbreak{}(16L)\$. Then \$r\_\allowbreak{}\{j+1\}/\allowbreak{}r\_\allowbreak{}j\textbackslash{}le1/\allowbreak{}8\$,\allowbreak{} and all later displacement is at most \$\textbackslash{}tau h\_\allowbreak{}j/\allowbreak{}(8L)\$. Translating a protected secant by this displacement changes its slope by at most \$\textbackslash{}tau/\allowbreak{}4\$. Thus every subgradient of the final common point \$y\$ has coordinate \$j\$ in \$[\textbackslash{}ell\_\allowbreak{}j-\textbackslash{}tau/\allowbreak{}4,\allowbreak{}u\_\allowbreak{}j+\textbackslash{}tau/\allowbreak{}4]\$. The midpoint vector differs from every such subgradient by at most \$3\textbackslash{}eta/\allowbreak{}4\$ in Euclidean norm. All probe and protection points lie within \$\textbackslash{}zeta\$ of the original point. The scales may be very small,\allowbreak{} but are positive and require the same finite number of queries.\newline{}\newline{}For a globally Lipschitz convex function and a public projected set \$K\textbackslash{}subseteq B\_\allowbreak{}2(R)\$ containing zero,\allowbreak{} the extracted vector satisfies\newline{}\$\$f(z)\textbackslash{}ge f(x)+\textbackslash{}langle\textbackslash{}widehat g,\allowbreak{}z-x\textbackslash{}rangle-2L\textbackslash{}zeta-2R\textbackslash{}eta\textbackslash{}quad(z\textbackslash{}in K).\$\$\newline{}Choose \$\textbackslash{}zeta=\allowbreak{}\textbackslash{}varepsilon/\allowbreak{}(16L)\$,\allowbreak{} \$\textbackslash{}eta=\allowbreak{}\textbackslash{}varepsilon/\allowbreak{}(16R)\$,\allowbreak{} so the model error is \$\textbackslash{}varepsilon/\allowbreak{}4\$ and \$\textbackslash{}|\textbackslash{}widehat g\textbackslash{}|\textbackslash{}le2L\$ in the stated nontrivial range. Projected subgradient descent with step \$R/\allowbreak{}(2L\textbackslash{}sqrt N)\$ gives averaged gap at most \$2LR/\allowbreak{}\textbackslash{}sqrt N+\textbackslash{}varepsilon/\allowbreak{}4\$. Taking \$N\textbackslash{}ge64A\textasciicircum{}2\$ proves the convex rate. The probes may leave \$K\$ only in the all-space variant.\newline{}\newline{}For a function defined on the ball,\allowbreak{} keep iterates in \$B\_\allowbreak{}2(R-2\textbackslash{}delta)\$. For strong convexity,\allowbreak{} apply extraction to \$h(x)=\allowbreak{}f(x)-\textbackslash{}mu\textbackslash{}|x\textbackslash{}|\textasciicircum{}2/\allowbreak{}2\$,\allowbreak{} which is convex and at most \$2L\$-Lipschitz because \$\textbackslash{}mu R\textbackslash{}le L\$. Choose \$\textbackslash{}delta=\allowbreak{}\textbackslash{}gamma/\allowbreak{}(16L)\$,\allowbreak{} vector error \$\textbackslash{}eta=\allowbreak{}\textbackslash{}gamma/\allowbreak{}(8R)\$,\allowbreak{} and add \$\textbackslash{}mu x\$ back. Then \$\textbackslash{}|\textbackslash{}widehat g\textbackslash{}|\textbackslash{}le4L\$ and\newline{}\$\$f(z)\textbackslash{}ge f(x)+\textbackslash{}langle\textbackslash{}widehat g,\allowbreak{}z-x\textbackslash{}rangle+\textbackslash{}mu\textbackslash{}|z-x\textbackslash{}|\textasciicircum{}2/\allowbreak{}2-\textbackslash{}gamma.\$\$\newline{}With \$a\_\allowbreak{}t=\allowbreak{}2/\allowbreak{}[\textbackslash{}mu(t+1)]\$,\allowbreak{} projection,\allowbreak{} and \$D\_\allowbreak{}t=\allowbreak{}\textbackslash{}|x\_\allowbreak{}t-x\_\allowbreak{}*\textbackslash{}|\textasciicircum{}2\$,\allowbreak{}\newline{}\$\$f(x\_\allowbreak{}t)-f(x\_\allowbreak{}*)-\textbackslash{}gamma\textbackslash{}le\textbackslash{}frac\{\textbackslash{}mu(t-1)\}4D\_\allowbreak{}t-\textbackslash{}frac\{\textbackslash{}mu(t+1)\}4D\_\allowbreak{}\{t+1\}+\textbackslash{}frac\{16L\textasciicircum{}2\}\{\textbackslash{}mu(t+1)\}.\$\$\newline{}Multiply by \$t\$ and sum. The initial distance coefficient is zero,\allowbreak{} and the remaining distance terms telescope. The weighted average has gap at most \$32L\textasciicircum{}2/\allowbreak{}[\textbackslash{}mu(T+1)]+\textbackslash{}gamma\$. Taking \$\textbackslash{}gamma=\allowbreak{}\textbackslash{}varepsilon/\allowbreak{}8\$ and \$T+1\textbackslash{}ge128L\textasciicircum{}2/\allowbreak{}(\textbackslash{}mu\textbackslash{}varepsilon)\$,\allowbreak{} including shrinkage loss at most \$2L\textbackslash{}delta\$,\allowbreak{} proves the result. Ordinary convex projected descent gives the \$A\textasciicircum{}2\$ branch. Deterministic value localization supplies the separate \$d\textasciicircum{}2\textbackslash{}log(ed)\textbackslash{}log(4A)\$ branch;\allowbreak{} take the minimum only among applicable branches.\newline{}\newline{}For a known body \$B\_\allowbreak{}2(r\_\allowbreak{}\{\textbackslash{}rm in\})\textbackslash{}subseteq K\textbackslash{}subseteq B\_\allowbreak{}2(R\_\allowbreak{}\{\textbackslash{}rm out\})\$,\allowbreak{} the identity \$(1-a)K+aB\_\allowbreak{}2(r\_\allowbreak{}\{\textbackslash{}rm in\})\textbackslash{}subseteq K\$ supplies feasible probe room. Choose \$a=\allowbreak{}\textbackslash{}gamma/\allowbreak{}(16LR\_\allowbreak{}\{\textbackslash{}rm out\})\$ and probe radius at most \$ar\_\allowbreak{}\{\textbackslash{}rm in\}/\allowbreak{}2\$. Shrinkage costs at most \$LaR\_\allowbreak{}\{\textbackslash{}rm out\}\$. The query count is independent of the probe radius and uses \$R\_\allowbreak{}\{\textbackslash{}rm out\}\$ in place of \$R\$. A finite-sum mean value costs \$n\$ component values,\allowbreak{} multiplying these deterministic bounds by \$n\$.\par\endgroup

\begingroup\raggedright\sloppy A public feasible point whose objective gap is at most \$G\_\allowbreak{}0\$ solves every target \$\textbackslash{}varepsilon\textbackslash{}ge G\_\allowbreak{}0\$ with exactly zero calls.\newline{}\newline{}For a convex mean objective that is \$L\$-Lipschitz on a ball of radius \$R\$,\allowbreak{} the center has gap at most \$LR\$. A sample Lipschitz modulus \$G\$ with \$\textbackslash{}mathbb E G\textasciicircum{}r\textbackslash{}le L\textasciicircum{}r\$,\allowbreak{} \$r>1\$,\allowbreak{} implies \$\textbackslash{}mathbb E G\textbackslash{}le L\$,\allowbreak{} so the same certificate applies to moment models. Integrability at one point ensures that the mean is defined.\newline{}\newline{}If a globally \$\textbackslash{}beta\$-smooth objective has a global minimizer within distance \$R\$ of the public initial point,\allowbreak{} its gradient vanishes at that minimizer and the smoothness inequality gives gap at most \$\textbackslash{}beta R\textasciicircum{}2/\allowbreak{}2\$. In a declared norm,\allowbreak{} use the corresponding radius in that norm. For \$B\_\allowbreak{}p(R)\$ with Euclidean regularity this radius is \$R\$ when \$p\textbackslash{}le2\$ and \$R d\textasciicircum{}\{1/\allowbreak{}2-1/\allowbreak{}p\}\$ when \$p\textbackslash{}ge2\$.\newline{}\newline{}For a known positive semidefinite quadratic matrix \$A\$,\allowbreak{} the center has gap at most \$\textbackslash{}lambda\_\allowbreak{}\{\textbackslash{}max\}(A)R\textasciicircum{}2/\allowbreak{}2\$;\allowbreak{} if \$A=\allowbreak{}0\$,\allowbreak{} the loss is identically zero. A public initial-gap promise \$\textbackslash{}Delta\$ directly gives the certificate \$G\_\allowbreak{}0=\allowbreak{}\textbackslash{}Delta\$. For the Markov potential \$r\_\allowbreak{}0\$,\allowbreak{} its companion initial iterate has gap at most \$\textbackslash{}mu r\_\allowbreak{}0\$. These are different certificates with different model assumptions;\allowbreak{} in particular,\allowbreak{} an unknown matrix with no public spectral bound does not acquire a uniform certificate.\newline{}\newline{}Call counts are nonnegative. Together with the stated algorithm,\allowbreak{} this proves exact zero complexity on each certified region. The upper/\allowbreak{}lower ratio is undefined,\allowbreak{} so it is stored as null rather than as \$0/\allowbreak{}0\$.\par\endgroup

\begingroup\raggedright\sloppy Write A=\allowbreak{}LR/\allowbreak{}epsilon>1. Upper bound:\allowbreak{} start with [a,\allowbreak{}b]=\allowbreak{}[-R,\allowbreak{}R]. Query u=\allowbreak{}a+(b-a)/\allowbreak{}3 and v=\allowbreak{}b-(b-a)/\allowbreak{}3,\allowbreak{} charging both exact scalar values. If f(u)<=\allowbreak{}f(v),\allowbreak{} retain [a,\allowbreak{}v];\allowbreak{} otherwise retain [u,\allowbreak{}b]. Convexity ensures that the retained closed interval contains a constrained minimizer,\allowbreak{} including in the equality case. After k steps its length is 2R(2/\allowbreak{}3)\textasciicircum{}k. Its midpoint is feasible and is within R(2/\allowbreak{}3)\textasciicircum{}k of a retained minimizer,\allowbreak{} so its objective gap is at most LR(2/\allowbreak{}3)\textasciicircum{}k. Taking k=\allowbreak{}ceil(log(A)/\allowbreak{}log(3/\allowbreak{}2)) gives a deterministic budget of 2k values and requires no value at the output. The finite comparisons and affine updates are Borel. This proves O(log(4A)) deterministically and hence also for the randomized 2/\allowbreak{}3 guarantee.\newline{}\newline{}Lower bound for every A>1:\allowbreak{} f\_\allowbreak{}+(x)=\allowbreak{}Lx and f\_\allowbreak{}-(x)=\allowbreak{}-Lx are admissible on [-R,\allowbreak{}R]. Their epsilon-success sets satisfy x<=\allowbreak{}-R+epsilon/\allowbreak{}L and x>=\allowbreak{}R-epsilon/\allowbreak{}L respectively,\allowbreak{} and are disjoint when epsilon<LR. A zero-query output distribution is common to both objectives;\allowbreak{} its two success probabilities sum to at most one. Thus the randomized 2/\allowbreak{}3 guarantee,\allowbreak{} and also the deterministic guarantee,\allowbreak{} require at least one scalar-value query.\newline{}\newline{}Logarithmic lower bound:\allowbreak{} use the subclass transfer in accepted local proof ZO\_\allowbreak{}PROOF\_\allowbreak{}PRECISION\_\allowbreak{}LOG,\allowbreak{} with its primary premise independently reread here. Dorn et al.,\allowbreak{} arXiv:\allowbreak{}2610.00345v1,\allowbreak{} source SHA256 1869dd758da361249e15ca5c9bc20792f55d6d7432b04be0d818323539baf105,\allowbreak{} Section 2 characters 6700-11900,\allowbreak{} Theorem 2.5 characters 13496-15396,\allowbreak{} and Theorem E.5/\allowbreak{}Section E.4 characters 112800-119800,\allowbreak{} uses a fixed worst-case budget and pointwise success probability 2/\allowbreak{}3 for arbitrary adaptive randomized exact-value algorithms. Its queries and outputs are unrestricted. The dimension-times-depth lower argument applies for d=\allowbreak{}1 as well. Set source localization radius R\_\allowbreak{}h=\allowbreak{}R/\allowbreak{}2,\allowbreak{} smoothness beta\_\allowbreak{}h=\allowbreak{}2L/\allowbreak{}(3R),\allowbreak{} and strong convexity mu\_\allowbreak{}h=\allowbreak{}beta\_\allowbreak{}h/\allowbreak{}2. Every source function has a global minimizer x\_\allowbreak{}* in [-R/\allowbreak{}2,\allowbreak{}R/\allowbreak{}2]. Since its gradient vanishes there,\allowbreak{} for |x|<=\allowbreak{}R we have |f'(x)|<=\allowbreak{}beta\_\allowbreak{}h(|x|+|x\_\allowbreak{}*|)<=\allowbreak{}L. Restriction to [-R,\allowbreak{}R] is therefore an admissible target function,\allowbreak{} and its constrained minimum equals its global minimum. A target algorithm can be simulated with one source value per target value,\allowbreak{} and its feasible output is permitted by the stronger source model. The source ratio beta\_\allowbreak{}h R\_\allowbreak{}h\textasciicircum{}2/\allowbreak{}epsilon equals A/\allowbreak{}6. Theorem 2.5 consequently gives T>=\allowbreak{}(3/\allowbreak{}4000)[1+log(A/\allowbreak{}6)/\allowbreak{}log(3)] when A>=\allowbreak{}A\_\allowbreak{}0=\allowbreak{}6*128\textasciicircum{}2=\allowbreak{}98304. This lower bound includes deterministic algorithms.\newline{}\newline{}Uniform combination:\allowbreak{} for A>=\allowbreak{}A\_\allowbreak{}0,\allowbreak{} log(A/\allowbreak{}6)>=\allowbreak{}log(4A)/\allowbreak{}2,\allowbreak{} since A\_\allowbreak{}0>=\allowbreak{}144. For 1<A<A\_\allowbreak{}0,\allowbreak{} T>=\allowbreak{}1>=\allowbreak{}log(4A)/\allowbreak{}log(4A\_\allowbreak{}0). Thus throughout A>1,\allowbreak{} T>=\allowbreak{}c log(4A),\allowbreak{} with c=\allowbreak{}min\{1/\allowbreak{}log(4A\_\allowbreak{}0),\allowbreak{}3/\allowbreak{}(8000 log(3))\}>0. Together with the ternary-search upper bound this proves Theta(log(4A)) for both quantities. At A=\allowbreak{}1 the existing zero-query comparison applies;\allowbreak{} the new region is strict and does not include that endpoint. Any overlap with an existing high-accuracy comparison specializes to compatible bounds,\allowbreak{} while its higher-dimensional claims are untouched.\par\endgroup

\begingroup\raggedright\sloppy Primary premise:\allowbreak{} Dorn et al.,\allowbreak{} arXiv:\allowbreak{}2610.00345v1,\allowbreak{} Section 2 and Theorem 2.1,\allowbreak{} archived SHA256 1869dd758da361249e15ca5c9bc20792f55d6d7432b04be0d818323539baf105,\allowbreak{} source characters 8930-11780 (theorem begins at 10190). For globally beta\_\allowbreak{}h-smooth convex objectives with a global minimizer in B\_\allowbreak{}2(0,\allowbreak{}R\_\allowbreak{}h),\allowbreak{} fixed-budget adaptive randomized exact-value algorithms with per-objective success at least 2/\allowbreak{}3 require T>=\allowbreak{}max\{5d/\allowbreak{}16,\allowbreak{}(d/\allowbreak{}4096)min\{d,\allowbreak{}sqrt(beta\_\allowbreak{}h R\_\allowbreak{}h\textasciicircum{}2/\allowbreak{}epsilon)\}\} when epsilon<=\allowbreak{}beta\_\allowbreak{}h R\_\allowbreak{}h\textasciicircum{}2/\allowbreak{}32. Queries and outputs may be unrestricted.\newline{}\newline{}Set R\_\allowbreak{}h=\allowbreak{}R and beta\_\allowbreak{}h=\allowbreak{}L/\allowbreak{}(2R). For every source objective choose a global minimizer x\_\allowbreak{}* with norm at most R. Its gradient vanishes. On B\_\allowbreak{}2(0,\allowbreak{}R),\allowbreak{} ||grad f(x)||\_\allowbreak{}2<=\allowbreak{}beta\_\allowbreak{}h ||x-x\_\allowbreak{}*||\_\allowbreak{}2<=\allowbreak{}2 beta\_\allowbreak{}h R=\allowbreak{}L. Integrating along segments in the ball proves that the restriction is convex and L-Lipschitz. Its constrained minimum equals the source global minimum.\newline{}\newline{}A target algorithm on this restricted objective is simulated using exactly one source scalar evaluation for each target value. The ball-restricted queries and feasible,\allowbreak{} possibly unqueried output are allowed by the stronger source model. The output gap and private-seed success probability are unchanged,\allowbreak{} and the same fixed worst-case cap holds on every path. Thus a uniformly successful target randomized algorithm would solve every source instance. Deterministic algorithms are included as seed-independent algorithms.\newline{}\newline{}Here beta\_\allowbreak{}h R\_\allowbreak{}h\textasciicircum{}2/\allowbreak{}epsilon=\allowbreak{}A/\allowbreak{}2,\allowbreak{} so the theorem window is exactly A>=\allowbreak{}64 and gives T>=\allowbreak{}max\{5d/\allowbreak{}16,\allowbreak{}(d/\allowbreak{}4096)min\{d,\allowbreak{}sqrt(A/\allowbreak{}2)\}\}. Since min\{d,\allowbreak{}sqrt(A/\allowbreak{}2)\}>=\allowbreak{}min\{d,\allowbreak{}sqrt(A)\}/\allowbreak{}sqrt(2),\allowbreak{} this proves Omega(d min\{d,\allowbreak{}sqrt(A)\}) with universal constants. No new target smoothness or global-minimizer promise is imposed:\allowbreak{} these are properties only of an adversarial subclass.\newline{}\newline{}On each existing R2 domain d>=\allowbreak{}d\_\allowbreak{}0,\allowbreak{} A>=\allowbreak{}C,\allowbreak{} A\textasciicircum{}2>d,\allowbreak{} retain the accepted lower Omega(d\textasciicircum{}2/\allowbreak{}log(ed));\allowbreak{} retain the independent accepted Omega(d log A) only when A>=\allowbreak{}98304;\allowbreak{} add this new lower only when A>=\allowbreak{}64. Their maximum gives the displayed three-branch lower envelope. Below 64 the old envelope remains unchanged,\allowbreak{} and equality at 64 is included by the source theorem. At A=\allowbreak{}d\textasciicircum{}2 and d tending to infinity the new lower is Omega(d\textasciicircum{}2),\allowbreak{} while the stronger old term is Omega(d\textasciicircum{}2/\allowbreak{}log(ed));\allowbreak{} the improvement is material. Upper bounds and logarithmic-gap labels remain valid;\allowbreak{} the gap expressions are recomputed as their upper envelope divided by the new compatible lower maximum.\newline{}\newline{}For A\textasciicircum{}2<=\allowbreak{}d and A>=\allowbreak{}64,\allowbreak{} the new d sqrt(A) rate is dominated by the accepted d A\textasciicircum{}2/\allowbreak{}log(e A\textasciicircum{}2) rate;\allowbreak{} no R1 change is needed. The zero-query region epsilon>=\allowbreak{}LR is disjoint from A>=\allowbreak{}64. At d=\allowbreak{}1 the transferred constant lower is dominated by the accepted Omega(log(4A)) one-dimensional envelope. Old lower-bound proofs and literature are retained conditionally,\allowbreak{} rather than recertified.\par\endgroup
